desc:
Given a non-empty binary tree, look at its deepest level (the level furthest from the root). Return the value of the leftmost node on that level.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [2, 1, 3, 4, -1, 5, 6, -1, -1, 7] the deepest level contains only the node 7, so the answer is 7. For tree = [2, 1, 3] the deepest level is [1, 3] and the answer is 1.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Only the last level matters. How would you know which level is the last one?
In a level-order array the levels appear one after the other, so the last real node belongs to the last level. But the leftmost node of that level is not necessarily near the end of the array.
Track the depth of each node. Whenever you see a depth for the first time, remember that node's value as the leftmost of that depth. The remembered value of the largest depth is the answer.
editorial: Do a breadth-first pass, left to right. The first node you meet on a new level is the leftmost node of that level. Overwrite your stored candidate every time a new level starts; after the last node has been processed the candidate belongs to the deepest level.
A depth-first search works too (visit the left child first and record a value only when a strictly deeper level is reached), but the level-order array makes a single linear scan the simplest.
